newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM heads to Toronto for summit with Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM heads to Toronto for summit with Fujimori.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto departed for Toronto on Friday for a meeting with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori to search for a peaceful end to the Lima hostage crisis.

A Japanese government source said Japan and Peru were united about not giving in to terrorism but divided over whether the time had come to give ground on the rebels' main demand that Peru free hundreds of their imprisoned comrades.
About 15 members of the Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) took over the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on December 17, seizing hundreds of hostages.
Most hostages have been released but 72 are still held.
Talks to secure their release appear bogged down by Fujimori's refusal to allow the question of the rebels' demand for the freeing of imprisoned comrades to even be raised at the negotiating table.
The Japanese government source said Hashimoto would urge Fujimori at their weekend meeting to soften his stance against the rebels and move ahead with direct negotiations with them.
"We are worried that there could be an unexpected development. Direct negotiations must be held soon," the source said.
Peruvian police repeatedly played loud tapes of martial music, sirens and the roar of aircraft outside the building on Thursday in an apparent ploy to wear down the rebels.
But the tactic has also unnerved Japan, which fears the rebels may lose patience and take their anger out on the hostages.
"It is vitally important that Japan's intention be fully reflected (at the summit) in overall measures to deal with the crisis," the source said.
The source said Hashimoto, who was due to leave Japan for Toronto on Friday evening, would urge Fujimori to give top priority to steps to secure the safe release of the hostages.
Earlier this week, Hashimoto called on Fujimori to exercise caution in the deployment of police at the site to prevent "accidents or incidents".

Though both the Peruvian government and the rebels have voiced willingness to sit down to discuss a peaceful end to the crisis, Fujimori has ruled out starting talks until the rebels drop their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
The rebels have said there is no point in talking unless that demand is on the agenda.
The Japanese government source said the Peruvian government should include the rebels' main demand on the agenda.
"But that doesn't mean that the imprisoned MRTA guerillas will be freed," the source said.
Shortly before leaving for Toronto on Thursday, Fujimori said in Lima that the meeting was aimed at achieving "a very close coordination".
"If we were in an emergency situation we would need to be in close contact," Fujimori said in an interview with Argentina's CVN television network.
